t.1.42.1: When that god of gods had departed, he, O Rāma, pressing down the earth with the tip of his big toe, remained in worship for a year.
t.1.42.2: Then, when a full year had passed, Umāpati Paśupati, revered by all the worlds, spoke these words to the king.
t.1.42.3: I am pleased with you, O best of men; I will do what is dear to you. I will bear upon my head the daughter of the king of mountains.
t.1.42.4: Then Haimavatī, the eldest daughter of Himavat, revered by all the worlds, assumed an exceedingly vast form and an unbearable force, and fell from the sky, O Rāma, onto the auspicious head of Śiva.
t.1.42.5: Bewildered within the circle of his matted locks, she could find no way out at all; the goddess wandered about right there for many long years.
t.1.42.6: O Raghunandana, Hara was exceedingly pleased by him, and then he released Gaṅgā toward Bindusaras.
t.1.42.7: From the sky she came to Śaṃkara's head and from there down to the earth; there the water spread forth, heralded by a tremendous roar.
t.1.42.8: Then the divine seers, Gandharvas, Yakṣas and hosts of Siddhas gazed there at her as she came down from the sky to the earth.
t.1.42.9: With aerial chariots shaped like cities, with horses and with excellent elephants, and also mounted on gliding conveyances, the deities stood there.
t.1.42.10: That fall of Gaṅgā, supreme and most wondrous in the world: eager to behold it, the hosts of gods of boundless might would gather together.
t.1.42.11: With the hosts of gods swooping down, and by the radiance of their ornaments, the cloudless sky shone as if it held a hundred suns.
t.1.42.12: Then the sky became filled with hosts of porpoises and serpents and with darting fish, flung about like flashes of lightning.
t.1.42.13: With white jets of water scattering in a thousand directions, the sky looked as though it were strewn with autumn clouds and with flocks of swans.
t.1.42.14: In some places it rushes on more swiftly, in some places it runs winding, in others stretched out straight; here it is bent low, there tossed upward, and in some places it moves along slowly, slowly.
t.1.42.15: In some places, water struck again by water itself rose up again and again along an upward path and fell back once more upon the earth.
t.1.42.16: That water, having fallen from the head of Śaṃkara and fallen once more upon the surface of the earth, then shone forth, pure and freed from all impurity.
t.1.42.17: There the hosts of ṛṣis and the gandharvas, and those who dwell upon the surface of the earth, touched the water that had fallen upon the body of Bhava, thinking it to be purifying.
t.1.42.18: And those who, because of a curse, had fallen from the sky to the surface of the earth, having bathed there, became freed of their sins.
t.1.42.19: Then, their sins washed away once more by that brilliantly shining water, they entered the sky again and attained their own worlds.
t.1.42.20: The people, delighted, rejoiced in that radiant water; having bathed in the Gaṅgā, they became free from weariness.
t.1.42.21: The royal sage Bhagīratha, of great splendor, mounted a divine chariot and went on ahead, and Gaṅgā followed behind him.
t.1.42.22: All the gods together with the hosts of sages, the Daityas, Dānavas and Rākṣasas, the foremost of the Gandharvas and Yakṣas, along with the Kiṃnaras and the great serpents,
t.1.42.23: O Rāma, all the Apsarases and all the creatures that move in the water, following Bhagīratha's chariot, went joyfully after Gaṅgā.
t.1.42.24: Wherever King Bhagīratha went, there followed the glorious Gaṅgā, best of rivers, destroyer of all sins.
